content:
I wonder if it would a nice feature if one could enable some sort of warnings on use use of classical theorems (e.g. if we want to stay constructive). For instance in this code

import Mathlib

theorem t1 (a : ℕ) : ¬¬ a = a := by
  simp only [not_not]

theorem t2 (a : ℕ) : ¬¬ a = a := by
  simp only [Decidable.not_not]

would be nice if the first theorem produces a warning about classical use in the elimination direction of Classical.not_not or at least lists nonconstructive use in the #print axioms t1.

I dont quite understand your last point, you will get Classical.choice in print axioms if it was actually used. Beyond that Introducing general warnings for use of classical axioms is possible but an explicit non-goal in Lean core.

You can do this yourself for your own project.
Write a style linter that runs #print_axioms on your declaration and raises a warning when it depends on choice.

If you are interested in staying constructive you may be interested in this paper (you can ignore the mathematics we formalized, but we explain how we were able to write constructive proofs using mathlib in a reasonable way).

Great work @Riccardo Brasca and it definitely builds on top of showing the Classical.choice in `#print axioms .... But how about the law of excluded middle and Classical.not_not above? At least the header docstring of the linter says:

The "detectClassical" linter emits a warning on declarations that depend on Classical.choice and/or sorryAx."

Maybe there is some argument related to Diaconescu-Goodman-Myhill theorem at play here (we only have AC -> LEM from my very limited understanding about this) or Classical.not_not is detected in some other way from your linter or not detected at all?

When it says "depend on Classical.choice", it means transitively. There are no other classical axioms provided by Lean or Mathlib, and so any theorem that can reasonably be considered classical is so because it uses choice internally.
Hmmm, I would also consider any theorem using Classical.not_not.mp nonconstructive and thus classical as well.
I suggest you reread my message and see what #print axioms has to say about Classical.not_not

Yes, this is what I thought too at first with my "AC -> LEM" statement above - that using Classical.not_not will warn about using axiom of choice and as such detecting all theorems that use the AC will result in detecting all theorems that use Classical.not_not but this is wrong conclusion at least theoretically.

While I can see this done in implementation here (#print axioms Classical.not_not), the DCM theorem is about AC -> LEM and not the other way around. This means that we could only conclude contrapositively not AC -> not LEM and there could still be theorems that use LEM without AC which will not be detected this way.

Forgive me if I lack some significant foundational detail here, I am just trying to understand if the implementation works on par with theory and is properly theoretically justified.
The linter emits a warning on anything that depends on excluded middle (and similarly on anything that depends on choice in any way). Is this what you want?

By this I mean that if declaration A is proved using choice, and B is proved using A, the linter will emit a warning in the proof of B. Excluded middle is A, it has nothing special in Lean, it is just a theorem (that depends on choice).

Ok, so indeed this is all about difference between Lean and a general abstract axiomatic framework. Essentially one can always axiomatize LEM separately, example in practice being ZF, but Lean has proven Classical.not_not entirely transitively from Classical.choice so detecting that should be sufficient and thus the linter will work just fine detecting potential uses specifically of Classical.not_not as a theorem.

I guess it is reasonable not to expect the linter to detect any custom implementation of not_not (or worse yet any shot at axiomatization) so @Riccardo Brasca's solution is indeed the closest to what I was originally looking for. Thanks to @Eric Wieser and @Riccardo Brasca for the extra follow-ups here!

I still don't understand what you want. Can you give a precise example of a case where the linter does not do what you want? With a bit of metaprogramming almost anything is possible, but we need to understand what you want.

I think I explained my final conclusion above, let me know if any specific point there is not clear or you have specific questions above them.

-> In one sentence, one can still use a foot gun by introducing separate LEM axioms that are not derived from axiom of choice but your linter should be good enough for all sane cases.

Sure you can introduce any new axiom. This would be shown in #print axioms of course, so if you want you can turn the linter the other way around and flag any theorem that depends on something else than propext and Quot.sound. The implementation is really pretty easy.
